rv.q: This production, directed with superb acerbity by Joe Mantello, marks the playwright's overdue Broadway debut, and it doesn’t disappoint.
Excellent performances and simple yet moving writing make Little Bear Ridge Road an all-around solid family drama.

It’s a hard-hitting, hard-laughing show that combines topics that you arrive at the theater not itching to confront — the COVID pandemic, meth addiction, health insurance, shift pay — into an absorbing story you leave wanting much more of.
Even by Metcalf’s lofty standards, this is one stunner of a performance.
Spending time with them means confronting our own shadows and asking some of life’s most nagging questions.

As played by a glorious Laurie Metcalf in Samuel D. Hunter’s keen-eyed, compassionate play “Little Bear Ridge Road,” which opened on Thursday night at the Booth Theater, she is also one of the funniest and most thoroughly human characters seen lately on a New York stage.
The show is at its best when allowing Ethan and Sarah’s relationship to unfold without forcing the revelations.
Hunter captures how slippery time felt in that period—infinity measured out in season finales.

I couldn’t escape the nagging sensation, as I watched Samuel D. Hunter’s drama unfold, that the circumstances were all arrayed too perfectly for a Metcalf showcase, that they’re too custom-fitted to her skills—that there were diminishing returns to watching her do only what she does best.

Hunter is a master at creating these types of indelibly flawed characters, and his sensitive writing is beautifully complemented by Joe Mantello's typically precise direction and the superb performances from the two leads.
It is both a powerful account of love misdirected and a bulletin from a hurting American heartland.
Only in a production directed by Joe Mantello of a play written by Samuel D. Hunter could a couch feel so cosmic.
On this small stage the real delight are the performances, and Hunter’s expertly crafted lines that Metcalf and Stock devour.

That plus a beautiful blend of gifted actors and director, a surprising amount of genuinely laugh-inducing humor, and even a soupçon of hope make for a thoroughly engaging 95 minutes, during which we find ourselves rooting for those we might otherwise want little to do with.
There’s hardly a better one to leave his mark on the neighborhood and, at least with this production, save it from becoming the existential cul-de-sac it threatens to become.
Every actor, including Meighan Gerachis (as Vickie) in a very small role as a hospice nurse, was dynamite, filling out the distorted humanity of each of their characters.
Little Bear Ridge Road is a touching, quietly lovely play about a few lonely people tentatively—and painfully—making emotional connections.

If you’re seeking purely escapist fare, you might just want to head next door to “Buena Vista Social Club.” But more adventurous theatergoers, or anyone who loves great acting, should definitely turn onto “Little Bear Ridge Road.”

Hunter play at Chicago's Steppenwolf Theatre last year. The reviews are rolling in for Samuel D. Hunter's Little Bear Ridge Road, which officially opened at the Booth Theatre October 30 after beginning previews October 7.

However, for all its occasionally touching vibes, smart repartee, and Laurie Metcalf’s expertise, the stakes in Hunter’s otherwise respectable dramedy aren’t high enough nor its conception novel enough to make it an especially memorable contribution to the Broadway catalogue.
Myself, I was happier when “Little Bear Ridge Road” wasn’t pretending to be anything more than a hilarious comedy about yet another dysfunctional family.
Joe Mantello masterfully and subtly directs Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock in two outstanding, compassionate performances in one of the best plays of the Broadway season so far.
Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock earn their Tony buzz in Little Bear Ridge Road, an intimate family drama about the ghosts we live with and the words we can’t say.
Hunter’s Broadway debut confirms what his Off-Broadway work has long suggested: he’s one of our finest writers of small lives rendered with enormous compassion.
Under the perfectly paced direction of Joe Mantello, the characters are so alive, even as they turn from fully living, that it is impossible to turn away.
Metcalf demonstrates why she is one of the finest actors of her generation — delivering a performance that is natural, compelling, and in key moments emotionally raw.

cn.t: Hunter's intimate Idaho drama earns strong praise for Metcalf's stunning performance and achingly human storytelling, though some critics find the minimalist production too small-scale. Most celebrate its quiet power and emotional authenticity.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.

vr.q: I really enjoy this play and I recommend it, but it's not my favorite Samuel J. Hunter play.
